method: An IPv6 delegation is split on power-of-two boundaries. A delegated prefix of length D carved into site prefixes of length S, with D <= S <= 64, gives 2^(S-D) site prefixes; each one holds 2^(64-S) subnets of length /64, so the whole delegation holds 2^(64-D) of those /64 subnets. The page does the split with 128-bit integer arithmetic: the delegation is aligned to its length (a prefix whose host bits are set is refused, and the aligned block is named in the error), site i starts at base + i * 2^(128-S), and the /64 range inside a site runs from that address to base + i * 2^(128-S) + (2^(64-S) - 1) * 2^64. IPv6 expects a subnet to be a /64 because interface identifiers are 64 bits long (RFC 4291, Section 2.5.1), which is why a site prefix longer than /64 is refused and every site is reported as an exact /64 range. The /56 default follows RFC 6177, the best-current-practice guidance on assignments to end sites, which recommends giving a site significantly more than a single /64 and names /56 as a reasonable default for home sites; /48 remains common for larger sites, and /64 is offered for a delegation that is itself a single subnet. Addresses are shown in the canonical RFC 5952 form (lower case, no leading zeros, the longest run of zero groups collapsed and a single zero group left alone); IPv4-embedded input such as 2001:db8::192.0.2.1 is accepted and rewritten in hex. Limits: a delegation length from 0 to 64, a site length from the delegation length to 64, and 1 to 64 sites listed (the first 16 are shown, with the count of the rest stated). Warnings appear when every site is a single /64, when the site prefix equals the delegation length so there is nothing to split, and when a site prefix shorter than /48 would hand out an unusually large block. The page plans a block it is given: it does not talk to a router or DHCPv6 server, does not verify that the prefix is delegated to the user, and does not configure router advertisements, SLAAC, routing or firewalls.
